title: Error Wrapping: errors.Is / errors.As
summary: Go errors are values. Wrapping with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` builds an **error chain** that adds context while preserving the original error. `errors.Is` checks whether a target error is anywhere in that chain; `errors.As` extracts a specific error *type* from it. Together they let you add context without losing the ability to inspect the cause.

subtopics.title: Wrapping with %w
subtopics.explanation: fmt.Errorf with the %w verb (exactly one per call in standard usage) returns a new error that both adds a message and remembers the wrapped error. The result implements Unwrap() error, returning the inner error. Using %v instead would format the text but break the chain — and preserving that chain is precisely what makes errors.Is and errors.As possible.

subtopics.title: errors.Is matches a sentinel
subtopics.explanation: errors.Is(err, target) walks the chain calling Unwrap, returning true if any error equals target (or reports Is(target) true). Use it for sentinel errors like sql.ErrNoRows or io.EOF — values you compare against, not types. It is the read side of the chain the %w verb builds.

subtopics.title: errors.As extracts a type
subtopics.explanation: errors.As(err, &target) walks the chain looking for an error assignable to *target's type; on a match it sets target and returns true. Use it when you need fields from a specific error type, like a *net.OpError or a custom *ValidationError. It is how you read data out of a wrapped typed error.

subtopics.title: Sentinel vs typed errors
subtopics.explanation: A sentinel is a package-level value (var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")) compared with errors.Is. A typed error is a struct implementing error that carries fields, matched with errors.As. Choose sentinels for simple known conditions, typed errors when callers need details — this choice decides whether callers reach for Is or As.

subtopics.title: Implementing Unwrap, Is, As
subtopics.explanation: A custom error joins the chain by adding Unwrap() error. You can also implement Is(target error) bool for custom equality, or As(target any) bool for custom extraction, but most code just embeds the wrapped error and provides Unwrap. That single method is what plugs your type into the same errors.Is/As machinery.

subtopics.title: Wrapping discipline
subtopics.explanation: Wrap at boundaries to add context ('querying user 42: ...'), but don't wrap so much that messages become noise. Decide whether an error is part of your API: if callers will errors.Is/As it, document the sentinel/type; otherwise consider not exposing it. errors.Join combines multiple errors into one so Is/As can match any of them.

foundations.overview: In Go, errors are ordinary values returned explicitly, not exceptions. As an error travels up the stack, each layer often wants to add context ('while saving order', 'while opening file') without throwing away what actually went wrong. Error wrapping solves this: fmt.Errorf with %w produces a new error that carries a message AND a link to the underlying error, forming a chain. errors.Is and errors.As then let callers inspect that chain — matching a known sentinel value or pulling out a specific error type — so you get rich context and precise handling at the same time.
foundations.formalDefinition: Error wrapping creates an error that implements Unwrap() error (or Unwrap() []error), linking it to one or more underlying errors. errors.Is reports whether any error in the chain matches a target value; errors.As reports whether any error in the chain is assignable to a target type and, if so, assigns it.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without wrapping, you either lose context (returning the bare error) or lose the cause (returning a new error with just a message). Wrapping keeps both. errors.Is/As replace brittle string matching on error messages with robust value/type checks — a frequent interview topic and a real-world reliability win.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an error chain as a stack of sticky notes on a package: each layer slaps on a note ('couldn't ship', 'couldn't fetch from warehouse', 'database down') but the package underneath stays intact. errors.Is is asking 'is the original problem THIS specific thing?'; errors.As is asking 'is any note actually a form I can read fields off of?'
foundations.runtimePerspective: Wrapping allocates a small wrapError struct holding the message and the inner error pointer. errors.Is and errors.As are simple loops that repeatedly call Unwrap() (or iterate the []error from errors.Join) until they find a match or reach the end. There's no magic — it's plain interface method dispatch and pointer chasing.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A repository layer returns fmt.Errorf("get user %d: %w", id, sql.ErrNoRows); the HTTP layer uses errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) to return 404. Network code uses errors.As to extract *net.OpError and decide whether to retry. Validation layers return typed *ValidationError carrying the offending field.
foundations.businessImpact: Precise error classification drives correct responses — 404 vs 500, retry vs fail-fast — which directly affects user experience and how incidents are triaged. Good error context slashes mean-time-to-resolution because logs explain what happened, not just that something did.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Standard wrapping and Is/As give a whole codebase one consistent error-handling vocabulary, replacing ad-hoc string comparisons that silently break when a message changes.
foundations.performanceImpact: Wrapping is a cheap allocation; Is/As are short linear walks of a usually-short chain. The cost is negligible compared to the I/O that produced the error. Avoid building absurdly deep chains, and don't wrap in tight inner loops on the success path (there's no error to wrap there anyway).
commonUseCases: Adding context at layer boundaries with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)
Mapping sql.ErrNoRows to a 404 via errors.Is
Extracting a typed error's fields with errors.As

commonMisconceptions.myth: errors.Is and errors.As do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Is matches a specific error VALUE (sentinel) by walking the chain; As matches and extracts an error TYPE so you can read its fields.

commonMisconceptions.myth: %v and %w are interchangeable when formatting an error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: %w wraps and preserves the chain (so Is/As can find the cause); %v only formats the text and breaks the chain.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Comparing err.Error() strings is fine for branching.
commonMisconceptions.reality: String matching is brittle and breaks when messages change. Use sentinels with errors.Is or types with errors.As.

visualExplorer.title: How errors.Is walks the chain
visualExplorer.caption: errors.Is repeatedly calls Unwrap, comparing each link to the target until it matches or the chain ends.

config.intro: errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) on a doubly-wrapped error works like this:

steps.name: Compare the top error
steps.detail: Is checks the outermost error (e.g. 'handler: ...') against the target. No match, so continue.

steps.name: Unwrap one level
steps.detail: It calls Unwrap() to get the next inner error ('repo: get user 42: ...') and compares again. Still no match.

steps.name: Reach the wrapped cause
steps.detail: Unwrap again yields sql.ErrNoRows. This equals the target, so Is returns true.

steps.name: Custom Is hook
steps.detail: If a link implements Is(target) bool, Is calls it — letting an error declare itself equal to a target without identity.

steps.name: End of chain
steps.detail: If Unwrap eventually returns nil with no match, Is returns false. errors.As works the same way but tests type-assignability instead of equality.

codeLab.title: Classify a wrapped error
codeLab.instructions: A sentinel ErrNotFound and a typed *RetryableError{After int} are defined. Implement `Classify(err) (code int, retryAfter int)` returning (404,0) if the chain contains ErrNotFound, (503, e.After) if it contains a *RetryableError, and (500,0) otherwise. Check not-found first.
hints: Use errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) for the sentinel — it walks the whole chain.
For the typed error, declare var re *RetryableError and call errors.As(err, &re).

debuggingLab.title: errors.Is suddenly returns false in production
debuggingLab.symptom: Callers used to map a database miss to 404 via errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows). After a refactor it always returns 500.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The refactor switched the format verb from %w to %v. %v formats sql.ErrNoRows as text but does not wrap it, so the returned error has no Unwrap link. errors.Is walks the chain, finds nothing matching sql.ErrNoRows, and returns false — so every miss now falls through to 500.
commonMistakes: Using %v (or %s) instead of %w when you intend to preserve the cause.
Relying on the message text instead of the wrapped sentinel.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Restore the wrap so the chain is preserved.

theory.question: Explain the difference between errors.Is and errors.As, and when you'd use each.
theory.directAnswer: errors.Is(err, target) reports whether a specific error VALUE — a sentinel like sql.ErrNoRows or io.EOF — appears anywhere in the error chain; use it to branch on known conditions. errors.As(err, &target) reports whether any error in the chain is assignable to a specific TYPE and, if so, assigns it to target so you can read its fields; use it for typed errors that carry data, like *net.OpError or a custom *ValidationError. Both walk the chain via Unwrap.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two standard-library helpers for inspecting wrapped error chains — one by value, one by type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To let callers handle causes robustly without comparing error message strings, which break easily.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each repeatedly calls Unwrap (or iterates errors.Join's slice); Is compares for equality (or calls a custom Is method), As tests type-assignability (or calls a custom As method).

theory.whyImportant: Choosing Is vs As correctly is a classic Go interview check and underpins correct error handling.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler uses errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) to return 404, and errors.As(err, &netErr) to decide whether a network failure is worth retrying.

followUps.question: Why must the second argument to As be a pointer to the target?
followUps.answer: As needs a writable location to assign the matched error into, so you pass ⌖ passing the value by copy would give you nothing back.

followUps.question: Can an error customize matching?
followUps.answer: Yes — implement Is(target error) bool or As(target any) bool to define custom equality/extraction, which Is/As will call.

theory.question: What does the %w verb do, and how is it different from %v?
theory.directAnswer: %w, used in fmt.Errorf, wraps an error: the returned error both renders a message and implements Unwrap() to return the wrapped error, keeping it reachable via errors.Is/As. %v only formats the error's text into the message; it does not create an Unwrap link, so the underlying error is no longer discoverable in the chain. Use %w when callers may need to inspect the cause; %v when you only want a string and intend to hide the cause.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A formatting verb that turns fmt.Errorf into a chain-building wrapper.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To standardize error wrapping in the language (added in Go 1.13) so context and cause can coexist.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: fmt.Errorf detects %w and returns a wrapError (or a multi-error for multiple %w in newer Go) whose Unwrap returns the wrapped error(s).

theory.whyImportant: Mixing up %w and %v silently breaks errors.Is/As — a subtle, high-impact bug.
theory.realWorldExample: Switching %w to %v during a refactor caused all sql.ErrNoRows checks to fail, turning 404s into 500s in production.

followUps.question: Can you wrap multiple errors at once?
followUps.answer: Yes — fmt.Errorf supports multiple %w verbs (Go 1.20+), and errors.Join combines several errors so Is/As can match any of them.

followUps.question: Should you always wrap?
followUps.answer: No — only wrap to add useful context, and only expose a cause as part of your API if callers are meant to inspect it; otherwise consider returning an opaque error.

theory.question: How do errors.Join and multiple %w verbs create a multi-error tree, and how do errors.Is/As traverse it?
theory.directAnswer: errors.Join(errs...) (Go 1.20) returns an error whose `Unwrap() []error` returns the non-nil inputs, and fmt.Errorf with multiple %w verbs does the same — so an error is no longer a single chain but a TREE. errors.Is and errors.As handle both shapes: at each node they check the node itself, then if it implements `Unwrap() error` they follow that single link, and if it implements `Unwrap() []error` they recurse into every branch (depth-first). So errors.Is returns true if the target is found in ANY branch, and errors.As assigns the first matching type it reaches in that traversal. This lets one returned error carry several independent causes (e.g. a batch that failed in two ways) while Is/As still match any of them.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The multi-error (tree) form of wrapping via errors.Join or several %w verbs, and how the standard Is/As traversal covers it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some operations fail for multiple reasons at once (validating many fields, closing several resources); a single linear chain can't represent that, so Go added Unwrap() []error.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Is/As are recursive: test the current error, then dispatch on whether Unwrap returns a single error (follow it) or a []error (iterate each child, recursing). A joinError's Error() concatenates children's messages with newlines.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing errors are trees, not just chains, is current (1.20+) knowledge and prevents surprise when Is/As match a target buried in one of several branches.
theory.realWorldExample: A cleanup routine does `err := errors.Join(f.Close(), tx.Rollback())`; the caller can still errors.Is(err, sql.ErrTxDone) to detect the rollback problem even though a file-close error is also present.

followUps.question: What order does errors.As pick a match in a tree?
followUps.answer: It's a depth-first, pre-order traversal, so As assigns the first type-assignable error it encounters walking the tree in that order.

followUps.question: Can you use multiple %w in one fmt.Errorf?
followUps.answer: Yes, since Go 1.20 fmt.Errorf accepts multiple %w verbs and returns an error whose Unwrap() []error yields all of them, equivalent to joining them with surrounding context text.

theory.question: How do you design an error API — choosing between sentinels, typed errors, and opaque errors — and when do you implement custom Is/As methods?
theory.directAnswer: Treat your errors as API surface. Use a SENTINEL (var Err... = errors.New(...)) for a simple, fielded-less known condition callers branch on with errors.Is (like ErrNotFound). Use a TYPED error (a struct implementing error) when callers need data — a field, a code, a retry-after — matched with errors.As. Return an OPAQUE error (just `errors.New`/wrapped text with no exported identity) when callers should NOT branch on the cause; this keeps your implementation free to change. Implement a custom `Is(target error) bool` when you want an error to match a sentinel without pointer identity (e.g. any of your errors should count as a generic ErrTransient), and a custom `As(target any) bool` when extraction needs custom logic (e.g. adapting to a third-party target type). Only promote a sentinel/type to documented API when you truly intend callers to depend on it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A decision framework for exposing errors: sentinel vs typed vs opaque, plus custom Is/As hooks for non-default matching.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Every exported sentinel/type becomes a compatibility contract; choosing deliberately controls coupling while still giving callers the classification they need.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: errors.Is checks == and then calls a link's Is(target) if present; errors.As checks type-assignability and then calls a link's As(target) if present — so implementing those methods overrides the default value/type matching for your error.

theory.whyImportant: Over-exposing internal errors couples callers to your internals; under-exposing forces brittle string matching. Deliberate error API design is a senior-level distinction.
theory.realWorldExample: A payments package exports ErrDeclined (sentinel) and *RateLimitError{RetryAfter} (typed), but wraps its internal Stripe errors opaquely so callers can't couple to the vendor's error shapes.

followUps.question: Why implement a custom Is method instead of another sentinel?
followUps.answer: A custom Is lets a whole family of concrete errors report equality to one target sentinel (e.g. every timeout-ish error Is(ErrTimeout)) without callers holding a pointer to each specific instance.

followUps.question: How do you keep an error opaque yet still logged richly?
followUps.answer: Return a sanitized message externally while internally wrapping the real cause with %w and logging the full chain at the boundary, so operators see detail but callers/clients can't branch on internals.

scenario.question: Your service branches on error handling by doing strings.Contains(err.Error(), "no rows"). It works until a library updates its error message and your 404 logic silently breaks. How should this be designed instead?
scenario.directAnswer: Stop matching on message text. At the layer that knows the condition, return (or wrap with %w) a stable sentinel like sql.ErrNoRows or your own ErrNotFound, and have callers branch with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound). If callers need details, use a typed error and errors.As. This decouples handling logic from human-readable messages, which are free to change without breaking behavior.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Replacing fragile string matching with value/type-based error inspection.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Error messages are for humans and change often; control flow must depend on stable identities, not strings.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrap the cause with %w so the sentinel/type stays in the chain, then use errors.Is/As to detect it regardless of surrounding context.

scenario.whyImportant: String-matching errors is a common real-world fragility that breaks silently on dependency updates.
scenario.realWorldExample: A driver upgrade reworded its error text; teams relying on strings.Contains broke, while teams using errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) were unaffected.

followUps.question: What if the library doesn't export a sentinel or type?
followUps.answer: Wrap its error in your own sentinel/typed error at the boundary so the rest of your code depends on your stable identity, not the library's text.

scenario.question: Your handlers return wrapped errors straight to clients, so responses leak internal details like SQL fragments and file paths. But you still want those details in your logs for debugging. How do you design the boundary?
scenario.directAnswer: Separate the internal error chain from the external response at a single boundary (usually the HTTP/gRPC handler or a middleware). Internally, keep wrapping with %w so the full chain — SQL text, file paths, causes — is preserved and LOGGED at the boundary. Externally, map the error to a safe, opaque client message plus a stable code, deriving the code from the chain via errors.Is/As (e.g. errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) -> 404 + 'not found', unknown -> 500 + 'internal error' with a correlation ID). Never send err.Error() to the client. This gives operators rich context while clients see only sanitized, stable messages, and it centralizes the leak-prevention in one place rather than trusting every handler.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A boundary that logs the rich internal error chain but returns a sanitized, opaque error to the client.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Wrapped messages are for humans/operators and often contain sensitive internals; exposing them to clients leaks implementation detail and can aid attackers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: At the edge, classify the error with errors.Is/As to pick a client code/message, log the full wrapped err (and a correlation ID) internally, and write only the sanitized message + ID to the response.

scenario.whyImportant: Leaking SQL, paths, or internal structure through error messages is a common security and information-disclosure finding; centralizing sanitization fixes it systematically.
scenario.realWorldExample: An API middleware logs `log.Error(err, 'reqID', id)` with the full chain, then returns `{ code: 500, message: 'internal error', requestId: id }`; support correlates the ID to the detailed server log without the client ever seeing the SQL.

followUps.question: How does the client-facing message stay stable while internal wrapping changes?
followUps.answer: The external message is chosen from your own sentinels/typed errors via errors.Is/As, not from err.Error(), so rewording internal wraps never changes what clients receive.

followUps.question: How do operators still find the details for a given response?
followUps.answer: Attach a correlation/request ID to both the logged chain and the client response, so a support ticket referencing that ID maps directly to the full internal error in logs.

systemDesign.question: Design a service-wide error taxonomy that maps domain errors to HTTP/gRPC status codes in one central place using errors.Is/As, and also drives retry classification.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define a small, stable set of domain error kinds in one package: sentinels for fielded-less conditions (ErrNotFound, ErrConflict, ErrUnauthorized) and typed errors where callers need data (*ValidationError{Field}, *RateLimitError{RetryAfter}, a *TransientError for retryable failures). Every layer wraps lower-level/vendor errors into these with %w at its boundary, so the rest of the system depends only on your stable identities. Put ALL transport mapping in one function, e.g. `func HTTPStatus(err error) (int, clientMsg string)` and `func GRPCCode(err error) codes.Code`, implemented purely with errors.Is/As: check the most specific types first (As for *ValidationError -> 400), then sentinels (Is ErrNotFound -> 404, Is ErrConflict -> 409), then a default 500. Reuse the same taxonomy for retry classification: `func Retryable(err error) bool` returns true for errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) or an errors.As match on *TransientError, false otherwise. Centralizing means adding a new domain error updates mapping in exactly one place, and no handler branches on strings.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A single source of truth for domain error kinds plus centralized functions that translate them to transport codes and to a retryable/not decision via errors.Is/As.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Scattering status-code and retry logic across handlers leads to inconsistency and string matching; one taxonomy keeps mapping consistent and refactor-safe.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Layers wrap causes into stable sentinels/types with %w; central mappers run ordered errors.As (specific types) then errors.Is (sentinels) checks, falling back to 500; the retry classifier reuses the same predicates.

systemDesign.whyImportant: A consistent error taxonomy is what makes a large service's responses and retry behavior predictable and safe to evolve, and it's a common system-design discussion for Go backends.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A gRPC service routes every handler's error through `GRPCCode(err)`: *ValidationError -> InvalidArgument, ErrNotFound -> NotFound, *TransientError -> Unavailable (client retries), default -> Internal; adding a new ErrQuota only touches that one mapper.

followUps.question: Why check errors.As for specific types before errors.Is for sentinels?
followUps.answer: Typed errors are usually more specific than broad sentinels; checking them first ensures, say, a *ValidationError maps to 400 even if it's also wrapped alongside a generic error, giving deterministic precedence.

followUps.question: How do you keep the taxonomy from leaking vendor errors?
followUps.answer: Each adapter layer converts third-party errors into your domain sentinels/types at its boundary (wrapping the original with %w for logs), so central mappers only ever see your stable kinds, not vendor-specific ones.

coding.question: Implement `RetryClassifier(err) (retryable bool, retryAfter time.Duration)` that returns retryable=true and the RetryAfter for a wrapped `*TransientError{RetryAfter time.Duration}` (via errors.As), retryable=true with 0 for a wrapped context.DeadlineExceeded (via errors.Is), and false otherwise.
coding.thoughtProcess: Two distinct checks over the chain. First use errors.As to look for the typed *TransientError — if found, it's retryable and we can read its RetryAfter field. Otherwise use errors.Is against the sentinel context.DeadlineExceeded — retryable but no specific backoff, so return 0. Everything else is not retryable. Check the typed error first so we can surface RetryAfter; a nil err returns (false, 0) naturally since neither check matches.
coding.lineByLine: TransientError is a typed error carrying a RetryAfter hint and a wrapped cause; its Unwrap() links it into the chain so errors.As can find it even when wrapped with %w. In RetryClassifier we declare `var te *TransientError` and call errors.As(err, &te): on a match te points at the found error and we return (true, te.RetryAfter). If that fails we call errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded), which walks the chain for the deadline sentinel and, if present, returns (true, 0) since a raw timeout has no server-suggested backoff. Otherwise we return (false, 0). Checking As before Is means a TransientError's RetryAfter takes precedence and a nil error falls straight through to (false, 0).
coding.timeComplexity: O(depth) for each Is/As walk of the error chain.

followUps.question: Why check errors.As before errors.Is here?
followUps.answer: The typed *TransientError carries a specific RetryAfter we want to surface; checking it first ensures we return that backoff hint rather than the generic (true, 0) that the DeadlineExceeded branch would give.

followUps.question: How would you also honor context.Canceled as non-retryable?
followUps.answer: Explicitly return (false, 0) for errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) before the DeadlineExceeded check, since a cancel is an intentional stop, not a transient failure to retry.

coding.question: Implement a custom error type `QueryError{Query string, Err error}` that wraps an underlying error so errors.Is and errors.As both work through it.
coding.thoughtProcess: To participate in the error chain, the type must implement Error() string and Unwrap() error. Error() gives a contextual message; Unwrap() returns the inner Err so errors.Is/As can walk past QueryError to the cause. Returning *QueryError (pointer) lets errors.As(err, &qe) extract it and read Query.
coding.lineByLine: QueryError holds the query text plus the wrapped Err. Error() formats a readable message including the underlying error. Unwrap() returns e.Err — this single method is what links QueryError into the chain, so errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) can match the wrapped sentinel and errors.As(err, &qe) can extract the *QueryError to read Query. Using a pointer receiver and returning *QueryError is required so errors.As's pointer-to-pointer matching works.
coding.timeComplexity: O(depth) for an Is/As walk over the chain.

followUps.question: How would a caller extract the query that failed?
followUps.answer: var qe *QueryError; if errors.As(err, &qe) { log(qe.Query) } — As walks the chain and assigns the matching *QueryError.

followUps.question: When would you add a custom Is method?
followUps.answer: When you want this error to compare equal to a target without pointer identity — e.g. treating any QueryError as equal to a generic ErrQuery sentinel.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define your domain sentinels and typed errors in one place and treat them as part of your package's API. Wrap with %w at layer boundaries to add context; map errors to transport codes (HTTP/gRPC) in one central place using errors.Is/As.
productionDeepDive.performance: Wrapping is a cheap allocation and Is/As walk short chains; the cost is dwarfed by the I/O that produced the error. Avoid pathologically deep chains and don't construct errors on hot success paths.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Errors are values and safe to pass between goroutines. When fanning out, collect failures and combine with errors.Join so a single returned error preserves every cause for Is/As.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Decide retry vs fail-fast by inspecting the chain (e.g. errors.As for a retryable type, errors.Is for context.DeadlineExceeded). Stable sentinels make this logic robust against dependency message changes.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log the full wrapped error (it includes the whole context chain) at the boundary, and attach structured fields extracted via errors.As. Don't log-and-return the same error at every layer or you'll get duplicate noise.
productionDeepDive.security: Be careful not to leak internal details (file paths, SQL) to clients through wrapped messages; return a sanitized opaque error externally while logging the rich chain internally.

caseStudies.problem: Callers needed to distinguish 'no rows' from real failures.
caseStudies.solution: sql.ErrNoRows is a documented sentinel matched with errors.Is through wrapping.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires discipline to wrap with %w all the way up.
caseStudies.lessons: Stable sentinels plus %w wrapping make condition handling robust across layers.

caseStudies.problem: Code needed to know if a network error was a timeout or temporary to decide on retries.
caseStudies.solution: Typed errors like *net.OpError extracted via errors.As expose those properties.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Typed errors couple callers to a concrete type.
caseStudies.lessons: Use errors.As when callers must read fields; use errors.Is for simple known conditions.

keyTakeaways: fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error, adding context while keeping the cause reachable; %v only formats text and breaks the chain.
errors.Is matches a specific error VALUE (sentinel) anywhere in the chain; errors.As matches and extracts an error TYPE so you can read its fields.
A custom error joins the chain by implementing Unwrap() error; pass a pointer to As (errors.As(err, &target)).
Branch on errors with Is/As, never on err.Error() strings, and only expose sentinels/types you intend callers to depend on.
